issues.legal_issue: A junior member of a joint Hindu family may act as its manager and maintain an eviction suit when the senior member is unavailable in exceptional circumstances, and the tenant may be estopped from disputing that authority after accepting rent from the junior member.
material_facts: The senior family member had lived permanently abroad for a long time and was not in a position to manage the family property.
The senior member had given the junior member a power of attorney.
Neither the senior member nor any other family member objected to the junior member acting for the family.
The junior member had collected rent from the tenant, who had paid it to him.
issues.conclusion: The junior member could maintain the eviction suit as the family’s manager, and the tenant could not challenge that authority in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sunil Kumar v. Ram Prakash and Tribhovandas Haribhai Tamboli v. Gujarat Revenue Tribunal, the senior member ordinarily manages joint family property, but a junior member may do so in exceptional circumstances, including when the senior member is away and unlikely to return within a reasonable time, or has relinquished management. Narendrakumar J. Modi v. Commissioner of Income Tax recognizes that a senior member may give up management in favour of a junior member. Under Mohinder Prasad Jain v. Manohar Lal Jain, a co-owner may initiate eviction proceedings without the other co-owners’ consent unless an objection is raised. A tenant who has accepted the junior member’s collection of rent is estopped from disputing his authority in these circumstances.

rule.if: family_eviction_suit and senior_manager_unavailable and junior_member_authorized and no_family_objection and tenant_paid_rent_to_junior

predicates.family_eviction_suit: A member purports to act for a joint family in a suit seeking eviction of a tenant from family property.
predicates.senior_manager_unavailable: The senior family member responsible for managing the property is away or otherwise unable to manage it.
predicates.junior_member_authorized: The senior member has authorized the junior member to manage or act for the family.
predicates.no_family_objection: No family member objects to the junior member acting for the family.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_to_junior: The tenant has paid rent to the junior member who acts for the family.

issues.definition: When a junior member brings an eviction suit for the family, the senior manager is unavailable, the junior member is authorized, no family member objects, and the tenant has paid rent to the junior member, the junior member may maintain the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court that affirms the trial court’s decision may comply with its duty by giving a reasoned decision showing conscious consideration of the issues and evidence, without repeating the trial court’s reasoning in full.
material_facts: The first appellate court affirmed the trial court’s judgment after reconsidering the matter on remand.
Its judgment addressed the issues and contentions and contained findings supported by reasons.
The appellant did not identify specific issues that the first appellate court had failed to address.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court complied with Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and there was no ground to set aside its judgment for non-compliance.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a first appellate court to decide the appeal with due consideration of the matters in dispute. Under Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, an appellate court affirming the trial court ordinarily need not restate the evidence or repeat the trial court’s reasons if it expresses general agreement with them. Madhukar v. Sangram involved a reversal without consideration of the trial court’s grounds or the evidence, and was distinguishable where the first appellate court affirmed the trial court after reasoned consideration.

predicates.first_appeal_affirms_trial_judgment: The first appellate court affirms the trial court’s judgment.
predicates.appellate_judgment_shows_conscious_consi: The first appellate court’s judgment shows that it considered the appeal and the parties’ contentions.
predicates.appellate_judgment_gives_reasons_on_issu: The first appellate court records reasoned findings on the issues arising in the appeal.

issues.definition: When a first appeal affirms the trial judgment and the appellate judgment shows conscious consideration and gives reasons on the issues, the first appellate court complies with its appellate duty.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may increase the agreed rent by the amount permitted by law while an eviction petition is pending and an order directing monthly rent deposits remains in force, provided the landlord gives the required notice.
material_facts: An eviction petition was pending before the rent controller, and an order required the tenant to deposit rent monthly.
After the required period had elapsed, the landlord gave the tenant written notice of an intended rent increase.
The landlord later notified the tenant that the rent had been increased.
issues.conclusion: The landlord could increase the agreed rent during the pending eviction proceeding and while the rent-deposit order remained in force, after giving the required notice.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 6A and 8 of the Delhi Rent Control Act permit an increase in agreed rent at the prescribed interval and require written notice of the landlord’s intention to increase it. The right to give that notice and increase the rent is not suspended by a pending eviction proceeding or an order requiring monthly rent deposits.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_rent_control_proceeding and eviction_petition_pending and rent_deposit_order_in_force and increase_interval_elapsed and landlord_gave_written_increase_notice

predicates.landlord_tenant_rent_control_proceeding: The dispute concerns rent payable by a tenant to a landlord in a proceeding under rent-control rules.
predicates.eviction_petition_pending: An eviction petition is pending before the rent-control decision-maker.
predicates.rent_deposit_order_in_force: An order requiring the tenant to deposit rent periodically remains in force.
predicates.increase_interval_elapsed: The period required before a further rent increase has elapsed.
predicates.landlord_gave_written_increase_notice: The landlord gave the tenant written notice of the intended increase.

issues.definition: If a rent-control eviction petition and rent-deposit order remain in force, the required interval has elapsed, and the landlord gave written notice, the landlord may increase the rent during the proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may bring an eviction suit under general law without leave of the rent controller when a lawful rent increase takes the premises outside rent-control protection and the earlier rent-control eviction petition has been withdrawn.
material_facts: The monthly rent was increased after notice, and the increased rent exceeded the threshold for rent-control protection.
The landlord gave a notice terminating the tenancy.
The earlier eviction petition before the rent controller was withdrawn before the landlord filed the suit under general law.
issues.conclusion: The rent-control protection ceased to apply when the increased rent exceeded the coverage threshold, and the landlord could maintain the general-law eviction suit without leave of the rent controller.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(c) of the Delhi Rent Control Act excludes premises whose monthly rent exceeds the statutory threshold. Sections 6A and 8 permit a lawful rent increase after notice. D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India explains the legislative choice to limit rent-control protection by rent level. Ambalal Sarabhai Enterprises Ltd. v. Amrit Lal & Co. recognizes that a landlord’s rights under general law are available when rent-control protection is withdrawn. On these facts, the earlier rent-controller petition had been withdrawn before the general-law suit was filed, so leave was unnecessary.

rule.if: general_law_eviction_suit and lawful_rent_increase and premises_rent_above_coverage_limit and landlord_gave_increase_notice and tenancy_termination_notice_given and earlier_rent_control_petition_withdrawn

predicates.general_law_eviction_suit: The landlord brings a suit seeking eviction under general law rather than seeking relief in the rent-control proceeding.
predicates.lawful_rent_increase: The rent was increased in accordance with the applicable rules for rent increases.
predicates.premises_rent_above_coverage_limit: After the increase, the monthly rent exceeds the limit for rent-control protection.
predicates.landlord_gave_increase_notice: The landlord gave the tenant notice of the intended rent increase.
predicates.tenancy_termination_notice_given: The landlord gave the tenant notice terminating the tenancy.
predicates.earlier_rent_control_petition_withdrawn: The landlord withdrew the earlier rent-control eviction petition before filing the general-law suit.

issues.definition: When a landlord brings a general-law eviction suit after a lawful increase takes the rent above the coverage limit, gives the increase and termination notices, and has withdrawn the earlier rent-control petition, the suit is maintainable without controller leave.

issues.legal_issue: Filing an eviction suit under general law itself constitutes notice to quit, so a separate notice to quit under the law governing transfers of property is not required to obtain an eviction decree.
material_facts: The landlord filed a suit under general law seeking possession from the tenant.
The tenancy had been terminated by notice before the suit was filed.
issues.conclusion: A separate notice to quit under the Transfer of Property Act was unnecessary because filing the general-law eviction suit itself constituted notice to quit.
issues.legal_principle: V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal supports the principle that filing an eviction suit under general law itself operates as notice to quit; a separate notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is not necessary to obtain an eviction decree.

predicates.general_law_eviction_suit: The landlord files a suit under general law seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.landlord_seeks_possession_from_tenant: The landlord seeks possession of the premises from the tenant.

issues.definition: When a landlord files a general-law eviction suit seeking possession from a tenant, filing the suit suffices as notice to quit.
